Keywords: Tomb, Place, The

outputs.L1:
**Tomb of a Millionaire**

A multimillionaire, ladies and gentlemen—  
a resting place for the dead, where every year  
the usury of twenty-five thousand dollars  
is spent on upkeep and flowers  
to keep fresh the memory of the departed.

The merchant prince, now gone to dust,  
commanded in his written will,  
beneath the signed name of his last testament,  
that twenty-five thousand dollars be set aside  
for roses, lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips—  
for perfume and color, the sweetness of remembrance  
surrounding his last, long home.

(A hundred cash girls want nickels  
to go to the movies tonight.  
In the back stalls of a hundred saloons,  
women sit at tables, drinking with men  
or waiting for men who jingle loose silver dollars  
in their pockets.  
In a hundred furnished rooms, there is a girl  
who sells silk, dress goods, or leatherware  
for wages of six dollars a week.  
And when she pulls on her stockings in the morning,  
she is reckless about God, the newspapers, and the police—  
about the talk of her hometown  
or the names people call her.)
outputs.L2:
Here lies a wealthy man—  
a man worth millions—  
in a resting place where, each year,  
twenty-five thousand dollars is spent  
on maintenance and blossoms  
so that remembrance of him will not fade.

Before the powerful businessman became dust,  
he ordered in his signed final will  
that this annual sum be reserved  
for roses and lilacs,  
hydrangeas and tulips—  
for fragrance, beauty, and the tender persistence of memory  
surrounding the home in which he would remain forever.

(Elsewhere, a hundred female cashiers lack even the small coins  
needed for tonight’s motion pictures.  
In the secluded corners of a hundred bars,  
women sit drinking beside men  
or wait for men whose pockets rattle with spare silver dollars.  
In a hundred rented, furnished rooms,  
young women who sell silk, dresses, or leather goods  
live on weekly pay of six dollars.  
Each morning, as one of them draws on her stockings,  
she no longer cares what God, the press, or the police may think—  
nor what people in her hometown might say,  
nor what degrading name society gives her.)
outputs.L3:
A multi-millionaire’s tomb receives $25,000 every year for maintenance and fresh flowers. In his will, the wealthy merchant set aside money to ensure that roses, lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips would continually decorate his grave and preserve his memory.

This lavish treatment of the dead stands in sharp contrast to the poverty endured by many living working women. Low wages leave these women unable to afford not only necessities but also simple pleasures and comforts. As a result, some may feel compelled to enter exploitative relationships or turn to sex work to survive or obtain what their wages cannot provide.

The text therefore condemns a society that spends enormous sums honoring a wealthy man after his death while showing little concern for the needs and dignity of living people. The carefully tended tomb becomes a symbol of distorted social priorities: wealth is celebrated and preserved even in death, while vulnerable workers are neglected.
outputs.L4:
The poem offers a powerful critique of social and economic inequality by contrasting a millionaire’s lavishly maintained tomb with the poverty and exploitation endured by working women. The tomb is treated with care and respect: money ensures that it remains clean, beautiful, and protected from decay. Although the millionaire is dead and no longer capable of appreciating these efforts, his wealth continues to command attention. His social status survives him, allowing his memory and burial place to receive resources that many living people are denied.

Against this image of privilege, the poem presents working women whose lives are shaped by hardship, exhausting labor, and economic insecurity. Their bodies and dignity are sacrificed to a system that values profit more than human well-being. While the millionaire’s grave is carefully preserved, these women struggle to obtain basic necessities and recognition. The juxtaposition is deliberately ironic: society devotes wealth and labor to honoring a dead rich man while ignoring the suffering of living workers.

Through stark imagery, the poem exposes the distorted values of a class-divided society. Wealth does not merely provide comfort during life; it also controls how a person is remembered after death. Poverty, by contrast, makes the living socially invisible, even when their labor sustains the world around them. The women may contribute more through their work than the dead millionaire can, yet they receive less care, respect, and security.

Ultimately, the poem condemns a system in which money determines whose life—and even whose death—is considered valuable. The carefully maintained tomb becomes a symbol of enduring privilege, while the suffering women represent those exploited and forgotten by society. By placing these images side by side, the poet challenges readers to question a social order that preserves the dignity of the wealthy dead but fails to protect the dignity and needs of the living poor.
outputs.L5:
### The Tomb

At the edge of the village stood a place no one visited after sunset. Beneath an ancient oak, half-hidden by moss and tangled roots, lay the tomb of an unnamed traveler. No inscription marked the weathered stone—only a small carving of a bird in flight.

The villagers believed the tomb guarded a forgotten secret. Some said treasure rested inside; others claimed it held the memory of a lost kingdom. Yet those who approached it felt neither fear nor greed. Instead, they experienced a strange peace, as though the quiet place reminded them that every journey, no matter how long, must one day come to an end.

counterfactuals.output:
The poem is **“Graceland”** by Carl Sandburg. Because it was published in *Chicago Poems* (1916), it is in the public domain in the United States:

> **GRACELAND**
>
> Tombs of the millionaires,  
> A lot of them,  
> And there are trees and flowers around them.
>
> I remember the will of one man  
> Who left money to keep roses,  
> Lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips  
> Around his tomb when he was dead.
>
> And a lawyer who read the will said:  
> “If we all had flowers around our graves,  
> We would need more flowers than there are  
> In the world.”
